newsitem.title: ITALY: Iri units need change before privatising-new chief.
newsitem.headline: Iri units need change before privatising-new chief.

text.p: The new president-designate of state holding Iri said many parts of the industrial giant would have to be adapted before they could be privatised and some were likely to need foreign or domestic partners.

Gian Maria Gros-Pietro, who was named by the Treasury on Sunday as the new Iri chairman, told La Stampa daily newspaper he fully agreed with a Treasury mandate to "privatise and liquidate" the industrial holding.
"It's a mandate with which I am perfectly in agreement," he said in the interview.
"(At Iri) we need to privatise and in the major part of cases, that means things which can be privatised only after certain operations," he said.

"There are things which would be difficult to place on the market as they stand. Certainly there's (telecoms holding) Stet which is a first class utility. And for (motorway operator) Autostrade there's a certain amount of private interest," he said.
"But I couldn't possibly think of putting (state airline) Alitalia on the market as it is. For that company, just as for Finmeccanica, it needs a certain amount of preliminary work," he said.
Aliances would be needed as well, rather than just financial operations. These would have to be alliances with counterparties interested in a private future.
"I don't think it would be possible to find a partner adapted for Alitalia among Italian companies," he added.
"And it's clear the three years of our mandate for placing all this stuff are not exactly overgenerous," he adde.
Gros-Pietro has been nominated to replace chairman Michele Tedeschi and his appointment is due to be put to an IRI shareholders' meeting later on Monday. The Treasury is sole shareholder.
Gros-Pietro said that conditions were at present highly favourable to carrying out privatisations of Italian companies.

"The moment is the most promising it has been for many years to aspire to some result. This applies to privatisations which don't concern only IRI but also (oil group) ENI and (power utility) Enel," he added.
Privatisations had to fulfil several needs -- raise money for state coffers, contribute to the growth of the equity market and encourage companies to open up internationally.
Gros-Pietro said it may be more difficult for the government to retain a golden share in privatised companies in Italy than was the case in Britain.
"It (the golden share) is an excellent instrument to favour the transition from a state economy to the market," he said.
"But in Great Britain it was introduced when London was already the second equity market in the world and there were no problems in absorbing the supply (of privatisation issues)," he added.
"In Italy the situation is different, there are big problems of political feasibility," he added.
